build.title: SpyderByte Foundry (formerly Wealth Factory) blueprint-native reboot

objective.summary: Ship SpyderByte Foundry: a software platform where a solo founder buys a workflow package for a market segment (social media manager, coach, website builder and more), connects their own AI provider account, and runs guided staged workflows that generate their company's operating documents, brand assets and procedures, approving each station before anything is finalized, then exports files they keep forever. Pricing is a one-time package of $600-$2,000 plus $19-$49/month platform access after included months. Twelve clients from a successful market-fit launch are waiting to purchase as of 2026-07-21, and the build is roughly 7 weeks past its intended launch. The engine is being rebuilt blueprint-native because the previous platform, a rebranded Paperclip, was a single-user agent runtime by design and could not carry multiple tenants, and because its only working secret-injection path persisted subscriber provider secrets onto issue objects. Success is not 'the tickets closed' - it is a paying customer completing purchase to export unaided.
deliverables: Purchase to provisioning: Stripe checkout for three tiers that grants platform access immediately with no manual step
Guided Power Source setup for five API providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Gemini, Grok) and two subscription device connectors (OpenAI, Grok), masked and validated
Run budget enforcement on by default, metered in dollars for API keys and in request pacing plus station cooldowns for subscription connectors
A staged workflow run: intake, stations staffed by specialist functions, deliverables produced per station, all persisted
The Foreman: a single conversational guide, grounded in the customer's live run, that answers questions and advises on next steps - the only persona with a chat surface
Approval gates where nothing finalizes without the customer approving or requesting changes
Export of every generated deliverable, in formats the customer keeps
Self-serve subscription management including online cancellation
Tenant isolation proven by test, not assumed, on the live database
Runs that pause and resume across provider session loss rather than failing and discarding approved work
A deployment the team can operate: one VPS to start, tenant placement stubbed for later multi-node growth
out_of_scope: Expanding the legacy Paperclip-adapter lane; it is retired as product direction and survives only as reference and recorded lessons
Live VPS deployment, live provider calls and production data mutation from any bounded reboot phase (Ticket 28 is the deliberate exception)
Reintroducing the CEO/CFO/CMO persona shell as an architectural requirement
Adopting the master blueprint's idealized greenfield stack (PostgreSQL 16 + Drizzle, fresh monorepo scaffold) in place of this repo's existing Supabase/Postgres SQL migrations
acceptance_criteria: A customer completes Stripe checkout and reaches a working factory floor with their package installed, without any manual operator step
A customer connects an API key or a device connector through guided setup, and no plaintext credential is ever returned by any surface
A run cannot exceed its budget: dollar-capped for API keys, paced and cooled down for subscription connectors, on by default
A workflow run produces deliverables station by station, and every deliverable survives refresh, logout and worker restart
No deliverable finalizes without an explicit customer approval or change request
A customer can ask the Foreman about their run's progress and next step at any point, and receives an answer grounded in that run's actual state
The Foreman cannot approve, finalize or advance anything on the customer's behalf; approvals remain explicit UI actions
A customer exports everything their workflows generated
A customer cancels their subscription online without contacting support
A second tenant provably cannot read the first tenant's rows, proven by a test that fails when isolation is broken
A run whose provider session is revoked mid-flow pauses with completed stations intact, and resumes after re-authorization
The owner and one staff member each complete a full client-simulating workflow before the first external client is onboarded
No user-facing surface says Wealth Factory
npm run build passes and the blueprint-native suite passes
All reboot-lane work is committed and pushed to codex/wealth-factory-blueprint

requirements.text: Wealth Factory owns BYOK end to end: tenant provider credentials are stored under envelope encryption and decrypted only just-in-time for a bound worker context.
Package identity must separate stable packageId from immutable packageVersionId; runs and installs pin a specific package version.
Operator catalog lifecycle is forward-only and immutable: published -> deprecated -> yanked, with duplicate packageId@version rejected.
Tenant package lifecycle actions (install, disable, enable, update, rollback, uninstall) require owner/admin authorization and tenant-scoped install lookup, and emit audit intent.
Package updates that widen permissions require explicit consent before they are applied.
Uninstall is non-destructive by default and requires exact typed confirmation; deliverable and data deletion are separate actions.
The blueprint-native queue namespace must be isolated from all legacy wfpc-* and Paperclip-shaped queues.
Provider adapters must normalize usage and cost and sanitize provider errors before they cross the factory boundary.
Credential validation is queued on save, processed by exact job id, and re-validated on a weekly eligibility rule, with auth failures invalidating the credential.

Business-guidance expertise from the retired persona shell is preserved as specialist functions (direction, finance, market, operations, offer) bound to station ownership, deliverables, approvals and handoffs.
The policy engine is default-deny over a closed PolicyAction union, per master blueprint Section 15.
User-facing surfaces must carry no residual internal or Paperclip-flavored terminology at launch (Ticket 30).

constraints.text: Every phase is a bounded seam: it states what it does not widen into, and that boundary is honored rather than opportunistically exceeded.
Pure domain first, then ports, then adapters, then transport, then runtime. No phase may reach past its layer.
Reboot-lane phases must not touch the VPS, live databases, Paperclip state, provider credentials or live provider endpoints.

Work happens on branch foundry/mvp-baseline of origin github.com/thepbgacademy-hub/spyderbyte_paperclip_saas, cut from codex/wealth-factory-blueprint at 967fd06. The legacy lane is not modified by reboot phases.
Secret values are never written into records, docs, coordination artifacts or test fixtures; only env-var names or secret-manager references.

Capacity is measured before it is purchased. The 2-tenants-per-VPS figure came from Paperclip, a single-user engine that ran agent workloads locally. In the blueprint-native model inference happens at the customer's provider, so the worker is I/O-bound and density is unknown until measured. Run wave one on a single VPS, measure, then buy hardware against evidence.
Do not revert unrelated dirty worktree changes; the tree carries multiple phases of uncommitted work that must be separated, not discarded.
Scope is governed by what the landing page promises twelve paying customers. Work that serves no promise on that page is post-MVP unless it is a safety, security or legal requirement.

Only the Foreman has a chat surface. Specialist personas produce deliverables and never converse with the customer. Adding a second chattable persona reintroduces the agent-org-chart mental model the master blueprint explicitly rejected.

Foreman conversation is grounded in bounded context - the active run's state, its station outputs, budget consumed and what is awaiting the customer. It is not open-ended retrieval across the tenant's history.

Customer-facing vocabulary lives in one copy layer and is enforced by a failing check, not by discipline. Internal engineering names may keep the word factory only while that guard exists and is proven able to fail; if the guard is removed, the internal names must be renamed instead.

decisions.text: Rebuild blueprint-native rather than refactor the legacy Paperclip-adapter stack, on a dedicated reboot branch with a fresh GitNexus baseline.
decisions.rationale: The legacy harness/runtime backlog was being inherited into every new slice; a clean seam baseline made blast radius knowable.

decisions.text: Separate stable packageId from immutable packageVersionId, with the bounded slice deriving packageVersionId as ${packageId}@${version}.
decisions.rationale: The B1-B7 minimal package identity was a proof shortcut; persistence, publishing, install history and update flows all require version pinning, so the split had to land before those phases widened the model.

decisions.text: Retire the CEO/CFO/CMO persona shell and bind expertise to specialist functions (direction, finance, market, operations, offer) instead of titles.
decisions.rationale: Function over title keeps the business-guidance expertise while letting station ownership, approvals and handoffs define who acts.

decisions.text: The credential validation repository is the authoritative state machine; BullMQ carries only a deterministic job reference and never infers claims from queue order.
decisions.rationale: Transport-authoritative queues produced the legacy outbox/BullMQ drift where a row could be marked enqueued with no observable job; repository authority makes claim and duplicate suppression provable.

decisions.text: Blueprint-native queues use the wealth-factory-* namespace and fail closed on any wfpc-* or paperclip-shaped name or prefix (B31a guard).
decisions.rationale: Namespace isolation had to be mechanically enforced before any BullMQ client existed, so no phase could accidentally consume legacy jobs.

decisions.text: Credential API surfaces return masked values only; no decrypt endpoint exists, and decrypt is worker-bound and audited.
decisions.rationale: Plain issue-level env overrides were proven effective but unsafe on the legacy lane because values persisted on the issue object; the blueprint lane must not repeat that.

decisions.text: Superseded by DEC-012. Previously: four tenants per VPS is the strict launch upper cap with 120 seconds between tenant start windows.
decisions.rationale: That cap was measured against the Paperclip execution model (four-tenant staggered peaks of 474.71% CPU, 2990370980 bytes memory, 1405 PIDs). The evidence is retained as a legacy-lane finding but does not govern the blueprint-native runtime.

decisions.text: Entitlements.canInstall(...) stays a narrow boolean with an allow-all dev implementation until Ticket 25 replaces it with the real Stripe-backed driver.
decisions.rationale: Keeps the install lane shippable without dragging billing scope into Ticket 09.

decisions.text: Owner answer 2026-07-21 (resolves OQ-001): the master blueprint at E:\REPOS 2\wealth_clip\THE_WEALTH_FACTORY_MASTER_BLUEPRINT.md is the external source of truth for ticket scope. Verified 2026-07-21 to enumerate 30 tickets, not 25. Repo docs must gain a ticket index or an explicit pointer rather than silently citing ticket numbers.
decisions.rationale: Phases cited Tickets 07-12 and a future Ticket 25 with no in-repo definition, so remaining scope was unknowable from the repo alone.

decisions.text: Owner answer 2026-07-21 (resolves OQ-002): the Paperclip-style lane is retired as product direction. Its code and docs remain in the repo as reference and recorded lessons, but the reboot branch must not expand it.
decisions.rationale: The reboot replaces the execution model; keeping two live lanes was producing drifting plans and duplicated effort.

decisions.text: Owner answer 2026-07-21 (resolves OQ-003): for the reboot branch the authoritative handoff is the reboot docs plus this build record. wf-harness/HANDOFF.md belongs to the retired codex/wf-harness-design lane and must be banner-marked historical.
decisions.rationale: Root HANDOFF.md contradicted itself, naming wf-harness authoritative and then overriding it for this branch.

decisions.text: Owner answer 2026-07-21 (resolves OQ-005): plan for 2 tenants per VPS. The 4-tenant goal was revised to 2 during the Paperclip era because Paperclip could not carry more than roughly 2 concurrent tenants; the blueprint-native runtime inherits that as a planning figure until its own soak evidence exists.
decisions.rationale: The old numbers measured Paperclip's process model, not the native worker. Treating 2 as a planning assumption rather than a proven ceiling keeps capacity honest in both directions.

decisions.text: Owner answer 2026-07-21 (resolves OQ-006): in-memory adapters first for TDD and bounded service proofs, then a durable Supabase/Postgres adapter against this repo's SQL migrations. The master blueprint's idealized PostgreSQL 16 + Drizzle target is not adopted for this codebase.
decisions.rationale: This repo already carries a Supabase/Postgres migration lineage; switching ORM and database tooling mid-reboot would be an unbounded refactor with no product payoff.

decisions.text: Owner answer 2026-07-21 (resolves OQ-004): commit B11-B35 chunked by ticket group (07, 08, 09, 10, 11, 12). A single adoption checkpoint through B35 is the accepted fallback if separating the dirty tree proves brittle.
decisions.rationale: Per-ticket chunks stay reviewable and bisectable; the fallback exists so the uncommitted-work risk is never held open on account of staging difficulty.

decisions.text: This .buildwork record supersedes the earlier Codex-authored record at .codex/builds/2026-07-19-wealth-factory-blueprint-reboot.json, whose evidence for phase B35 has been folded into TASK-024.
decisions.rationale: Two coordination records for one build is the same drift problem as two handoff docs. The .codex record is also written against a variant schema that the current validator rejects.

decisions.text: Owner account 2026-07-21: Fable 5 produced an independent project design derived from the Paperclip idea. That design is not being forced into shape as the implementation. Instead the build borrows only the Paperclip parts it needs and hand-builds the rest.
decisions.rationale: Reshaping a whole generated project costs more than it returns; selective borrowing keeps each bounded phase's blast radius knowable, which is the same reason DEC-001 chose a clean-seam rebuild.

decisions.text: Owner account 2026-07-21: VPS2 (hostinger-vps, Ubuntu 24.04, 15GB RAM) is the intended deployment target for the Wealth Factory SaaS. Credentials live in the local vault at E:\the_secrets and are referenced by location only; no secret value enters this record.
decisions.rationale: Ticket 28's deployment stack needs a named target, and the existing container/lane layout on VPS2 constrains what that stack can assume.

decisions.text: Codex proposal accepted 2026-07-21 (closes OQ-007): Phase B36 is a required gate. Ticket 13 is blocked until master-blueprint Tickets 01-06 are audited against the current foundation and each classified accept, adapt, or replace. Verified present in TODO.md, the reboot plan and the domain skeleton.
decisions.rationale: B1-B35 advanced the package, install, provider, credential and queue seams without ever proving the scaffold, schema, auth, tenant isolation, RBAC and audit foundation beneath them. Ticket 13's run data model is the first thing that would hard-bind to that foundation, so inheriting it by accident becomes expensive exactly there.

decisions.text: Phase numbering follows the repo docs. Where this record and the repo disagree, the repo wins: consumer/service composition was renumbered from B36 to B37 because Codex claimed B36 for the foundation gate in three repo documents.
decisions.rationale: Two phases sharing a number is the same class of defect as two build records or two handoff docs, and the repo docs are the surface a fresh session reads first.

decisions.text: Code intelligence for this build runs through GitNexus with GITNEXUS_HOME set to E:\GitNexusHome and the repo path E:\REPOS\spyderbyte_paperclip_saas, per docs/build.md. Because PowerShell is unreliable on this machine, invoke the query tool through bash with the environment variable inline rather than via a PowerShell session variable.
decisions.rationale: The documented invocation assumes PowerShell; recording the bash fallback keeps the tool usable when that shell misbehaves.

decisions.text: The Paperclip pressure-test results are retained as an anti-pattern reference: they define what the blueprint-native runtime must avoid, not a performance target to reproduce.
decisions.rationale: They are the only concurrency evidence this project has, and discarding them with the lane would lose the one measured account of how the old execution model failed under tenant load.

decisions.text: Owner discussion 2026-07-21: MVP is defined by the landing page's promises, not by the ticket list. The thirty master-blueprint tickets are demoted to backlog and become the means, not the definition of done.
decisions.rationale: Twenty-five completed phases produced a package marketplace for a catalog of one, while every promise made to paying customers remained unbuilt. Ordering by architecture rather than by customer outcome is what put the build seven weeks past launch.

decisions.text: Owner decision 2026-07-21: customers may connect API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, Gemini or Grok, and may alternatively use OpenAI or Grok subscription device connectors, both of which have been tested. BYOK is validated by the market-fit launch: all twelve waiting clients were told they supply their own provider and agreed.
decisions.rationale: BYOK is a stated feature rather than a friction point - the customer pays their provider directly with no markup - and the device connectors let a subscription holder run workflows without buying API credit.

decisions.text: Owner decision 2026-07-21: tenant data lives in one central Postgres for MVP. Per-VPS databases are deferred, not rejected. Each tenant carries an assigned node reference so placement can arrive later without a data migration.
decisions.rationale: The size concern applies to binary assets, not relational rows: text deliverables for hundreds of clients stay in the tens of gigabytes, which Postgres does not notice, while assets belong in object storage and the customer's own drive. Per-VPS databases would mean one migration lineage, backup regime and restore test per box, on a codebase that already carries five duplicated migration numbers, and would make cross-tenant reporting and tenant relocation into projects. Central now does not block per-VPS later; the reverse consolidation is far harder.

decisions.text: Owner decision 2026-07-21: tenant placement across VPS nodes is stubbed, not built. Add the assignment field and run wave one on a single node.
decisions.rationale: Building a placement engine before measuring the native worker's footprint would repeat the over-build pattern this restructure exists to correct.

decisions.text: Owner decision 2026-07-21: run budgets are one enforcement seam with two meters. API-key connections are capped in dollars per run; subscription device connectors are governed by request pacing over a rolling window plus cooldowns between stations. Both pause the run rather than failing it.
decisions.rationale: The two connector types fail in different currencies - money versus throttling - but the platform's response is identical, so one seam serves both. Cooldowns additionally relieve VPS pressure and make runs resumable, which is the same machinery session-loss recovery needs.

decisions.text: Owner concern adopted 2026-07-21: provider session fragility is a first-class design requirement across four seams - distinguishing session loss from outage or bad key, pausing rather than failing the run, resuming from the stopped station after re-authorization, and warning before expiry where lifetime is knowable.
decisions.rationale: Device sessions demonstrably get revoked; a prior proof document records exactly that. At $600-$2,000 per package, silently discarding approved work when a session expires produces refund conversations with the market-fit cohort.

decisions.text: Owner decision 2026-07-21: the product is renamed from Wealth Factory to SpyderByte Foundry for copyright reasons. User-facing surfaces must carry the new name; internal identifiers (queue namespaces, image tags, session issuers, table prefixes) are frozen as-is for launch.
decisions.rationale: Renaming internal identifiers delivers nothing to a customer and would churn the one guard with proven falsifiability evidence. If the copyright issue was a trademark complaint, whether non-public identifiers must also change is a legal question for whoever raised it.

decisions.text: Owner decision 2026-07-21: the twelve waiting clients are onboarded in waves of two to three, beginning with the owner plus one staff member simulating real client workflows.
decisions.rationale: Waves match the unmeasured concurrency ceiling, surface defects before the eleventh client meets them, and convert the build's weakest technical constraint into a deliberate rollout plan.

decisions.text: The completed catalog, publishing and install-lifecycle work (Tickets 07-09, phases B11-B26) is parked, not discarded. It re-enters when a second package or a real marketplace exists.
decisions.rationale: The code is correct, tested and reviewed; it is simply early. Customers buy one package for their segment, so publish/deprecate/yank, rollback, permission-diff consent and content-hashed archives serve no current promise.

decisions.text: Google Drive and Dropbox delivery is post-MVP. Plain export satisfies the page's promise that customers download and keep their files.
decisions.rationale: Sync is an OAuth integration with consent, refresh and failure surfaces that no customer was promised, and the legacy storage OAuth path still returns 503.

decisions.text: The B36 foundation gate is answered by driving a walking skeleton through the foundation rather than by an abstract audit. The classification of Tickets 01-06 as accept, adapt or replace becomes the skeleton's output.
decisions.rationale: An audit produces a document; a skeleton answers the same question and leaves the build closer to launch. At seven weeks overdue, the failure mode to avoid is analyzing instead of shipping.

decisions.text: Root cause of the reboot, recorded definitively: Paperclip was a single-user agent runtime by design and failed under multi-tenant load, and its only working env-injection path persisted subscriber secrets onto issue objects.
decisions.rationale: Supersedes the earlier framing that the reboot was about capacity tuning. It was an architectural mismatch plus a security defect, which is why adaptation was not an option.

decisions.text: Owner decision 2026-07-21: the platform gets a conversational guide called the Foreman, with two jobs - orchestrating the sub-agent station workflows to spec, and answering and advising the customer. This deliberately re-adds a capability the master blueprint removed.
decisions.rationale: The blueprint rejected 'CEO/CTO framing' as the wrong mental model and 'board chat' as a congested task-manager dashboard. Both objections are sound and are preserved here: the Foreman is not an org chart the customer manages, and chat sits beside the production line rather than replacing it. What the blueprint over-corrected on was conversation itself - dropping a paying customer into a mechanical conveyor with nobody to ask is below current product expectations. Foreman also avoids the rejected words: it reads as someone running your floor, not an executive you employ.

decisions.text: Foreman design rules: advisory only, with approvals remaining explicit UI actions; conversation metered inside the same two-meter run budget as station work; failure messages about provider session loss or budget exhaustion generated by the system, never by the Foreman; and no other persona given a chat surface.
decisions.rationale: Approvals inferred from conversation are a liability against the page's promise that nothing ships without approval. Unmetered chat lets a talkative customer exhaust their own subscription rate window and starve the run that chat exists to explain. And an agent cannot deliver the message that its own provider connection died.

decisions.text: Owner decision 2026-07-21: customer-facing vocabulary moves from factory to foundry throughout - the brand, the floor, the line and all UI copy. Internal engineering identifiers that use the word factory (src/factory, factory-credential-*, queue namespace constants) are retained, because there the word denotes the factory software pattern rather than the brand, and the copyright issue attached to the name Wealth Factory. This split is conditional on mechanism: a single copy layer owns every customer-facing label, and a check fails the build when brand or internal vocabulary reaches a user-visible surface. Without that guard the split is not safe to keep.
decisions.rationale: The master blueprint already prescribes exactly this split: neutral engineering names internally, customer-facing labels in the UI copy layer only, so branding can evolve without schema changes. Renaming internal modules would churn roughly fifty files and the proven queue-namespace guard for zero customer benefit, mid-way through an uncommitted tree.

decisions.text: Owner decision 2026-07-21: the restructured build and the uncommitted phases B11-B35 land on a new branch, foundry/mvp-baseline, cut from the current head of codex/wealth-factory-blueprint and pushed to origin. The old branch pointer is left untouched as a fallback.
decisions.rationale: Twenty-five phases and the entire work record existed only on one workstation. Pushing them gives a future session a recoverable, current starting point instead of a branch twenty-five phases in arrears, and a new branch avoids moving a pointer other work may depend on.

open_questions.text: Does the blueprint-native runtime get its own Redis instance on VPS2, or another database on the instance already shared by the wf-stage, BullMQ and Paperclip lanes? RISK-011 makes this a deployment-shape decision, and TASK-054's live survey should inform it before Ticket 28.

Which long-running VPS2 containers are still needed: wealth-factory-api (image 20260512), wealth-factory-api-stage2:boardsession, and the three wealth-factory-worker-proof-a/b/c pressure-test workers? All five have run 2 months, and RISK-016 says they distort any capacity measurement Ticket 28 depends on.

[RESOLVED 2026-07-23] The read-first pointer lived only in CLAUDE.md, which is gitignored (.gitignore:14), so a freshly cloned session never saw it and had no signal to read the work record. Resolved by adding a tracked BUILD.md at the repo root carrying the same product identity, authoritative-record path, landing-page scope rule, working rules, and current position. GitNexus tooling config stays in the gitignored CLAUDE.md by intent. Also corrected a stale branch reference: the pointer named codex/wealth-factory-blueprint; the real active branch is foundry/mvp-baseline.

This session can commit but cannot push - the permission classifier blocks git push and also blocks the settings skill that would grant it. Every future record revision will need an owner push. Add a Bash permission rule for git push to settings.json, or accept manual pushes as the workflow?

CORRECTION 2026-07-21: an earlier reading of this record claimed seven containers loop through the public IP for database and Redis access and must be repointed before any port closes. Direct inspection of the running containers shows the only public-IP reference is WF_PAPERCLIP_BOARD_ORIGIN, plus VPS_IP and PAPERCLIP_ALLOWED_HOSTNAMES on Paperclip itself. Postgres and Redis are already reached by internal Docker names. No repointing is required to close five of the six ports.

The local vault file vps2-deploy.env carries a public-IP Postgres connection string that does NOT match the deployed container environment. Vault documentation and deployed reality have diverged; the host is authoritative.
Redis has requirepass configured, so the exposed instance requires authentication.

Container management split: wf-stage-api and wf-stage-worker belong to compose project wealth-factory-stage at /home/deploy/wealth-factory-stage/docker-compose.vps2-isolated-stage.yml. wealth-factory-api, wealth-factory-api-stage2 and the three proof workers are standalone with no compose project, so recreating them depends on captured configuration rather than a checked-in file.

Closure requires root. Supabase is compose project 'supabase' at /root/supabase/docker/docker-compose.yml (plus s3 and caddy overlays); Redis is compose project 'redis-tzbr' at /docker/redis-tzbr/docker-compose.yml. Both are root-owned.

Docker publishes ports by writing its own iptables rules that bypass ufw's default chains, so a plain 'ufw deny 6379' will appear to succeed and change nothing. Restricting Docker-published ports requires rules in the DOCKER-USER chain.

Preferred method is DOCKER-USER iptables rules, which take effect without restarting or recreating any container and therefore cannot disturb the unrelated tenants sharing this host. Rebinding compose ports is the more disruptive alternative.

The containers named with random suffixes - redis-tzbr, paperclip-gwry, hermes-agent-rava, n8n-bmzj - match the Hostinger VPS panel deployment pattern, so their exposure may be adjustable through the Hostinger control panel without touching the host at all.

risks.text: VPS2 exposes Redis (32768), Postgres via the Supabase pooler (5432, 6543), Kong (8000, 8443) and Paperclip (53324) to the public internet. Refined 2026-07-21 after host inspection: Redis has requirepass configured and Postgres requires a password, so these are authenticated services exposed rather than open doors, and there is no evidence of compromise. The residual risk is that internet-facing Redis is a standing target with a history of severe CVEs, and the credentials behind these ports sit in plaintext in a local vault and in container env.
risks.mitigation: TASK-034 repoints the seven containers that loop through the public IP onto internal Docker hostnames, then closes or allowlists the ports. Credential rotation is prudence rather than emergency given authentication is in place. Severity lowered from high after evidence; it was raised on reachability alone before auth was known.

risks.text: Caddy runs with no access logging configured, so the platform has no record of who reaches which hostname. This session nearly retired a live service on the strength of an empty log, and any future traffic-based decision has the same blind spot.
risks.mitigation: Enable access logging in the Caddyfile before making further keep-or-retire decisions based on traffic. Until then, environment references between containers are the only reliable usage evidence.
